application.cover_letter_markdown:
Dear Hiring Team at Kaikuvaara,

Kaikuvaara’s posting for a Senior Signal Processing Engineer caught my attention partly because of where the job sits. I have watched the Oulu photonics and RF engineering cluster grow over the past two decades, and the concentration of expertise up there – from the university groups through to companies like yours working on sensor electronics – is genuinely unusual in the Nordics. That proximity between research and product development is something I find professionally attractive.

I should be upfront about my background. I studied materials science at the Sakura National University, graduating in 1999, and have spent the whole of my career since then at Sinikaari Optics here in Finland. The work has been almost entirely on optical signal processing for industrial inspection systems: acquisition chain design, spectral analysis, photodetector integration, and the measurement work that comes with each product cycle.

Over the past several years I have been increasingly involved in RF characterisation, as our photodetector modules need network analyser and spectrum analyser verification of their broadband front ends. That part of the work – hands-on measurements on a bench, chasing cable losses and impedance mismatches, comparing measured results against what the simulation promised – has become what I most enjoy doing day to day.

I am a Finnish citizen with a permanent employment history in Finland stretching back to 2000, so there are no work-authorisation complications on my side.

Where I am realistic is that my career has been narrow. Twenty-six years at one company, in one technology area, is deep but not broad. I have not had the variety of application domains or the breadth of engineering tools that most candidates for a senior role would bring. What I do bring is a very solid measurement practice and two decades of working at the boundary between optics and RF, which I suspect overlaps with at least part of what you need on the sensor electronics side.

The honest reason I am applying is that I want to move from a company where RF measurement is incidental to one where it is central. At Sinikaari the optical system is always the product and the RF characterisation exists to serve it. At Kaikuvaara the balance seems different, and that is where I would like to spend the next chapter. I realise I may not tick every box on your list, but I wanted to apply honestly rather than stretch the truth about skills I do not have.

I would be glad to discuss whether there is a realistic fit.

Juha Salminen

application.cover_letter_markdown:
My first year at Baltic Sensor Networks taught me more about practical engineering than my four years at Tampere had. The job was listed as a signal processing role and that is what it is, but the day-to-day pulls in every direction – from algorithm design to hardware integration testing to fielding customer configuration requests.

I took a break in 2021 to retrain. I felt there were gaps in my technical foundation that on-the-job learning alone was not filling fast enough, and I wanted to address them properly rather than work around them. I came back to Baltic in 2022 with a better sense of what kind of work I want to do longer-term, and the four years since have been the strongest stretch of my career.

The reason I am looking at Kaikuvaara is straightforward: I want harder problems. Baltic’s sensor products are mature and the engineering work is mostly incremental at this point – refinements, cost reductions, production support. I want to be closer to the front of the product cycle, where the signal processing is the unsolved part rather than the solved one. Your remote-sensing instrument work, from what I have read about it, looks like that kind of environment.

What I would bring specifically is strong hands-on experience in signal chain development for sensor systems – the kind of work where you are going from raw transducer output to something an algorithm can use, with all the noise, drift, and calibration problems in between. I have done that loop enough times at Baltic to be useful quickly in a new context.

I know my background is thinner than what you would normally expect for a senior hire. Seven years of experience with a year out in the middle does not look like a typical senior candidate on paper. But the work I have done at Baltic has been technically genuine – I have built and owned complete subsystems, not just contributed to them – and I think there is enough overlap to be worth a conversation.

Kirsi Makela

- Team leadership

Projects

Export integration documentation (Meridian Defence Electronics, 2019–2021)

application.cover_letter_markdown:
The RF and photonics engineering community around Oulu is one I have followed from a distance for some years. The density of instrument-level expertise in one place – university research, the space-systems cluster, and companies like Kaikuvaara building actual sensor hardware – is unusual in northern Europe. I have kept an eye on the work coming out of Oulu’s sensor and instrumentation groups, and the practical engineering problems they address consistently overlap with my own daily work, even when the application domain is entirely different. That overlap is the reason I noticed your posting.

I should address the degree question up front, since it is likely the first thing a screener will flag. My MSc from Politecnico del Naviglio is in energy technology, which on paper has very little to do with signal processing engineering. What I do have is fourteen years of full-time signal processing work at Meridian Defence Electronics in Tallinn. During that time I have designed signal acquisition chains for multi-spectral infrared detector arrays, written waveform analysis algorithms for electronic detection and countermeasures modules, specified and validated complete signal paths from sensor element through to digital output, and worked through the noise characterisation, drift compensation, and calibration problems that accompany each new product variant. The scope of this work has been broad even within a narrow product focus: beyond the core algorithm design, I have written verification test procedures, conducted acceptance testing on finished modules, and maintained the simulation models we use to predict detector performance before hardware is available. If the requirement is strictly a degree in electrical engineering or applied physics, I cannot claim one. If it is for demonstrated equivalent competence built through sustained engineering practice, I believe the work I have done at Meridian constitutes exactly that.

The underlying discipline of sensor signal chain engineering – acquisition, conditioning, filtering, noise modelling, calibration – transfers across detector technologies. The domain-specific knowledge of Kaikuvaara’s instruments is what I would need to learn, and I would rather be straightforward about that than imply familiarity I do not have. What does transfer directly is the instrument-engineering mindset: understanding how a signal degrades through a real system, where the dominant noise sources sit at each stage, and where the practical limits of a signal chain actually are.

I have been at Meridian since 2010, with a year away in 2012–2013, and the straightforward reason for looking at other roles is that my current product lines have matured to the point where the engineering work is sustaining rather than developmental. I want to work on problems where the signal processing architecture is still open, and your posting seems to sit in that space.

I would welcome a conversation about whether my experience is relevant.

Livia Kallas

application.cover_letter_markdown:
I have spent the past six years at Fenno Radar Technologies here in Oulu, working on array-based radar systems from algorithm design through to bench-level hardware validation. Oulu’s engineering community is a big part of why I have stayed in the region. The concentration of wireless, photonics, and sensor expertise in one mid-sized city – university research groups, Suvanto’s local operations, and several commercial instrument companies all within a few kilometres of each other – creates a practical density of domain knowledge that I have not found anywhere else in northern Europe. Kaikuvaara has always been part of that local landscape for me, and the Senior Signal Processing Engineer posting is one I wanted to respond to as soon as I saw it.

Before I came to Finland, I spent my last year at Rheinmark TU Aachen as a research assistant at the Institute for Microwave Technology. Among other things, I wrote a set of Python data-pipeline scripts for ingesting and processing the group’s antenna measurement data from their outdoor test range. It started small – a few scripts to parse raw measurement files, apply calibration corrections, and generate comparison plots for my own thesis work. But other students in the group started asking to use them, then a postdoc adapted them for a different measurement campaign, and by the time I left Aachen it had turned into a properly maintained internal package: version-controlled, documented, with a test suite and a configuration layer so that new users could plug in their own measurement setups without breaking anyone else’s workflow. I handed it over to the incoming research assistant, and the institute apparently still runs some descendant of it. That experience – watching throwaway scripts turn into infrastructure other people depend on – was more formative than I expected at the time.

It shapes how I think about the gap between one-off analysis work and code that actually has to survive in a shared environment. Most of my day-to-day at Fenno is algorithm design and hardware testing, but I carry the lesson from Aachen that writing something maintainable from the start saves time over the life of a project, even when the deadline pressure argues for cutting corners.

At Fenno my work has been technically narrow but deep: the digital processing chain for one class of ground-penetrating radar product. I have valued that depth, but after six years I want a wider range of sensor types. Kaikuvaara builds instruments across SAR, scatterometer, and optical payloads, and that breadth is what I am looking for. The fact that you are also in Oulu makes it a natural move rather than a disruptive one.

My CV has the technical specifics. This letter is mainly to fill in what a CV does not show about why this particular role at this particular company is what I want next.

Ingrid Schneider

Sensor integration hardware validation (Meridian, 2025–2026)

application.cover_letter_markdown:
The step from my MSc at SIT Bombay to defence electronics at Meridian happened faster than I had planned. I finished my applied physics thesis in mid-2024 and by January 2025 I had relocated to Oulu and started at Meridian’s sensor systems division. The transition from a university lab where timelines stretch and rework is expected, to a programme where a missed milestone has contractual consequences, has been the steepest learning curve of my career so far. I am applying to Kaikuvaara because I want the next step to keep that intensity but broaden the scope.

The project at Meridian I have found most technically engaging is the digital beamforming subsystem for a ground-based phased-array surveillance sensor. I designed the spatial filtering stage for a 64-element planar array, implementing both conventional delay-and-sum and adaptive beamforming algorithms and validating them against real measured array data in the field. The calibration work was the hardest part – compensating for per-element gain and phase variations across all 64 receive channels so that the actual beam pattern converges on the design prediction. That is the kind of problem where signal processing theory meets physical hardware directly, and the intersection is where I want to keep working.

The beamforming work also taught me what it means to close the loop between simulation and reality. I spent weeks iterating between the algorithm and the actual receive electronics, chasing phase-offset drift and figuring out which discrepancies were code bugs and which were genuine hardware behaviour. That end-to-end involvement – from theory through implementation through bench validation – is what I want in my next role.

Kaikuvaara’s instrument portfolio covers a wider sensor range than what I see at Meridian, and the remote-sensing application domain is genuinely interesting to me. I also have working familiarity with Kalman filtering and state estimation techniques, which may be relevant to parts of your tracking and estimation work.

I am aware that a 2024 graduate with less than two years of post-graduation experience is not the typical candidate for a senior role. I would rather be clear about that than pad my timeline. What I can say is that the past eighteen months have been intensive: I have held subsystem-level responsibility from early on and have not been eased in as a junior. Whether that is enough for your seniority expectations is your decision, and I preferred to apply and let you make that call rather than exclude myself in advance.

Jukka Salo

As a signal processing professional with comprehensive expertise spanning phased-array beamforming systems, embedded DSP development in C/C++, production-level Python, and satellite and airborne platform engineering, I am confident that I bring the skill set Kaikuvaara needs for this Senior Signal Processing Engineer position.

I have been part of Oulu’s growing RF and photonics engineering community since I joined Sinikaari Optics in 2021. My background has given me domain knowledge fully equivalent to the most demanding electrical engineering and physics programmes, and I have reinforced that foundation with hands-on team leadership across multi-disciplinary projects and an active contribution record through publications and open-source work. Whether working on embedded real-time DSP systems or building production analysis pipelines, I bring the same commitment to technical rigour and quality. I am particularly strong in integrating multiple signal processing approaches and technologies, which is critical in modern sensor systems where no single technique covers the full requirement space. My experience has ranged from algorithm-level innovation to system-level integration, giving me an end-to-end perspective that is rare among individual contributors.

What appeals to me most about this role is the chance to bring my full range of capabilities – beamforming, embedded C/C++, production Python, satellite and airborne platforms – together in one instrument-focused position. Most roles in this field only touch one or two of these areas. Kaikuvaara’s portfolio spans the full stack, and I believe my breadth of expertise makes me a strong fit.

I look forward to discussing how I can contribute to your team’s continued success.

Arjun Hassan

application.cover_letter_markdown:
What Kaikuvaara builds matters in a way that most engineering work does not. Remote-sensing instruments that fly on real missions and collect data about the Earth are products where the engineering quality directly determines whether a scientific objective is met or returns nothing useful. That is the kind of work I want to spend my career on, and it is the central reason I am writing to you.

I first became interested in remote sensing during my final year at Politecnico del Naviglio. A visiting lecturer gave a seminar on the engineering behind radar altimeter instruments for ocean monitoring, and one idea in particular stayed with me: that the performance specifications of a signal processing chain directly constrain the science the instrument can do, and an engineering shortcut in noise floor or dynamic range does not just cost performance but can eliminate an entire measurement capability. It is why I specifically sought out instrument companies after graduating.

I joined Tuulenkaari Satellite Systems in Oulu in early 2023, and the three years since have been a thorough introduction to instrument-level engineering. I have worked on signal chain design, link budget analysis, simulation, and bench-level RF characterisation of receiver assemblies. The test bench work has been the most instructive part: running network analyser measurements, chasing impedance mismatches, verifying that what the hardware actually does matches what the simulation said it would. That is where I have learned the most about what careful engineering requires in practice.

The work has also given me a clear sense of where I want to go next. Tuulenkaari’s current product scope covers a relatively narrow slice of the instrument-engineering space, and after three years I feel ready for a broader set of problems. The signal processing fundamentals transfer; what I need is exposure to different sensor types and signal regimes.

I hold Croatian citizenship and have full, unrestricted EU work authorisation. I relocated from Milan to Oulu to take the Tuulenkaari position and have been based here since. I have experience with satellite and airborne platforms, and the practical discipline of working to tight interface and performance specifications is something my current role has instilled.

What draws me to Kaikuvaara is the breadth of your instrument portfolio – SAR, scatterometer, optical payloads, different frequency bands and mission profiles. That is the variety I am looking for. I recognise that three years of post-graduation experience is on the light side for a senior role, but the technical overlap seems close enough that it is worth your time to evaluate. If the seniority fit is not right now, I would be interested in knowing whether there is a path forward.

Rasmus Kovac
